parameters.text:
# What is a decision tree?

Imagine playing **20 Questions**. One person thinks of something, and your job is to figure out what it is by asking only yes/no questions. If you ask random questions, you'll waste turns quickly. But if you ask smart questions that split the possibilities—like "Is it alive?" or "Is it bigger than a car?"—you narrow down the options much faster. Each answer pushes you down a different path of reasoning until eventually you're confident enough to guess the object.

A **decision tree** in machine learning works in almost exactly the same way. The model learns a sequence of yes/no questions that progressively narrow down the possibilities. Each question splits the data into groups, just like how your questions in 20 Questions split the set of possible objects. As you move down the tree, the possibilities get more specific until you reach a final answer or prediction. In other words, a decision tree is basically the computer learning how to play a really efficient game of 20 Questions.

# How can a decision tree be used?

This idea becomes useful when we apply it to real data. Instead of guessing objects, the questions are about features in the data. For example, imagine a bank trying to decide whether to approve a loan. The model might start with a question like *"Is the applicant's income above $50,000?"* If yes, it follows one branch; if no, another. The next question might be *"Does the applicant have existing debt?"* or *"Is their credit score above 700?"* Each step narrows down the possibilities until the tree reaches a final decision, such as approving or rejecting the loan.

Because of this structure, decision trees can be used for many practical tasks. They are commonly used for **classification**, like identifying whether an email is spam or not, diagnosing diseases from symptoms, or recognizing objects in data. They can also be used for **prediction**, such as estimating house prices or customer churn. In each case, the model is essentially learning the most informative sequence of questions to ask about the data so that it can arrive at the most accurate answer.

# Terminologies

The connections between nodes are called **branches**, which represent the possible answers to each question, such as yes or no. For example, in a game like _Guess Who?_, asking "Do they wear glasses?" would create two branches: **yes** and **no**. These branches lead to the next set of questions, which can be called **split nodes**, where you continue narrowing down the possibilities with new questions like "Do they have blonde hair?" or "Are they wearing a hat?" Eventually, you reach **leaf nodes**, which represent the final outcome—when you've narrowed it down to a single character and can confidently make your guess.

![dtree_diagram](images/dtree_diagram.svg)

# The Iris Dataset

To see decision trees in action, we can use the **Iris dataset**, one of the most well-known datasets in machine learning. It contains measurements of iris flowers and the goal is to classify each flower into one of three species: **setosa**, **versicolor**, or **virginica**. <video src="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t-I9Zgafz4A" />

Each flower in the dataset is described using four features: **sepal length**, **sepal width**, **petal length**, and **petal width**. A decision tree can learn a sequence of questions about these measurements—such as "Is the petal length less than 2.5 cm?"—to progressively narrow down which species the flower belongs to. By following these splits, the tree can classify a new flower based on its measurements.

Let's look at a sample decision tree for this dataset and how you can predict off it!

# What just happened?

What just happened is that the algorithm **learned a sequence of questions** from the data that helps it distinguish between the three iris species. Using the training dataset, the decision tree examined the four features—sepal length, sepal width, petal length, and petal width—and searched for splits that best separated the different classes.

Starting from the root node, the algorithm chose a feature and threshold that divided the data into groups that were more "pure" (meaning they contained mostly one species). It then repeated this process for each resulting subset, creating more nodes and branches. This continued until the stopping conditions in the default scikit-learn settings were met.

The final result is a **tree of decision rules**. When you pass a new flower to the model, it simply follows the learned path of questions (for example, checking petal length, then petal width) until it reaches a leaf node, which gives the predicted species. In essence, the model has automatically learned how to play a structured version of 20 Questions for identifying iris flowers.

Now, let's see what hyperparams we can change!

parameters.text:
# Hyperparameters?

Now the difference is that you were able to control **how the tree learns** by adjusting its hyperparameters. Instead of letting the algorithm grow the tree freely, you placed limits on its structure—for example by setting a **maximum depth**.

This affects how complex the tree can become. If the tree is allowed to grow very deep, it may keep splitting the data until it almost perfectly memorizes the training set. While this can give very high **training accuracy**, the model may start capturing noise or very specific patterns that don't generalize well to new data. This is known as **overfitting**.

By limiting the depth (for example, max_depth = 3), the tree is forced to learn **simpler decision rules**. It may not perfectly classify every training example, but the rules it learns tend to generalize better. This is why you might observe something interesting: the model with a limited depth can sometimes produce **better accuracy on the test set**, even though it performs slightly worse on the training set. In other words, restricting the model's complexity can help it make better predictions on unseen data. 

Now, create your own set of training questions! No worries, the relevant information will be provided to you.

# Congratulations!

In this step, instead of letting the algorithm decide the splits, **you chose the questions yourself** and manually built the tree. In other words, you played the role of the decision tree algorithm.

Starting from the root, you selected a feature and a threshold to split the data—for example, a question like "Is petal length less than 2.5 cm?". Each time you added a question, you divided the dataset into smaller groups and continued asking new questions to further separate the species. Eventually, each path ended with a final prediction.

This activity highlights what the algorithm normally does automatically: it searches through many possible questions and selects the ones that best separate the data. By building the tree manually, you can see how each question affects the dataset and how good questions quickly narrow down the possibilities—very similar to choosing effective questions in games like _20 Questions_ or _Guess Who?_.

# What just happened?

When you made a prediction, the decision tree followed a path through its learned questions based on the flower measurements you provided.

Starting at the **root node**, the tree checked the first condition—for example, "Is the petal length less than 2.5 cm?"—and took the branch corresponding to your input. It then evaluated the next condition along that branch, and so on, until it reached a **leaf node**. The species label at that leaf is the prediction you saw.

The key insight is that the tree already knows all its questions—it learned them from training data. When predicting, it doesn't re-learn anything; it simply **routes your input** through the fixed set of rules until it arrives at an answer. The highlighted path you saw in the visualisation is exactly the sequence of questions the tree asked about your specific flower.
